reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: Superficial vein thrombosis is thrombosis with associated inflammation of a superficial vein, most often affecting varicose tributaries of the great saphenous vein in the lower limb and presenting as a tender, erythematous, palpable cord

Once regarded as benign, it is now recognised to carry a meaningful risk of concurrent or subsequent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, particularly when extensive or lying close to the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junctions

Whole-leg compression ultrasound is advised to define thrombus extent, measure the distance to the deep venous junction and exclude coexisting deep vein thrombosis, which is present in a notable minority at diagnosis

Anticoagulation at prophylactic intensity for a defined period (for example fondaparinux or low-molecular-weight heparin) is recommended for thrombosis of significant length lying away from the junction, whereas thrombus close to or extending into the deep system warrants therapeutic anticoagulation as for deep vein thrombosis
Migratory or recurrent thrombophlebitis affecting otherwise normal veins (thrombophlebitis migrans, the Trousseau sign) should prompt evaluation for occult malignancy or thromboangiitis obliterans
Mondor disease denotes superficial vein thrombosis of the thoracoabdominal or breast wall veins; it is usually self-limiting, but breast wall involvement warrants exclusion of an underlying carcinoma

Upper limb superficial vein thrombosis is most often related to intravenous cannulae or infusions, and a suppurative (septic) thrombophlebitis must be distinguished as a separate infective emergency requiring antibiotics and sometimes vein excision
reference.pathophysiology: Superficial vein thrombosis develops through the components of the Virchow triad acting on a superficial vein: venous stasis (typically within tortuous varicosities), endothelial injury (from cannulation, trauma or chemical irritation) and hypercoagulability. Thrombus forms within the lumen and provokes an inflammatory response in the vein wall and surrounding tissue, producing the characteristic tender, indurated, erythematous cord. When the process involves the great or small saphenous trunk it can propagate proximally and extend through the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction into the deep venous system, or shed thrombus to the pulmonary circulation, which underlies the recognised association with deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
additionalDifferentials: Cellulitis or other soft tissue infection
Insect bite or localised hypersensitivity reaction
additionalInvestigations: Whole-leg duplex ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis, map extent and measure distance to the deep junction
Duplex assessment for coexisting deep vein thrombosis
Thrombophilia screen in selected patients with recurrent, unprovoked or unusual-site thrombosis
Evaluation for occult malignancy when the pattern is migratory or unexplained
Full blood count and inflammatory markers if a septic (suppurative) process is suspected
Venous reflux (varicose vein) studies to assess underlying chronic venous disease
Blood cultures and imaging for suppurative thrombophlebitis where infection is likely
redFlags: Thrombus extending towards or across the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction
Pleuritic chest pain or breathlessness suggesting pulmonary embolism
Fever, purulence or fluctuance indicating suppurative (septic) thrombophlebitis
Migratory pattern raising suspicion of underlying malignancy
reference.prognosis: Most localised superficial vein thrombosis settles over a few weeks with conservative measures and, where indicated, a course of anticoagulation. However, proximal extension and venous thromboembolism can occur, and recurrence is common in those with varicose veins or an underlying thrombophilia.
pitfalls: Dismissing the condition as trivial and missing a concurrent deep vein thrombosis or junctional extension
Failing to image the whole leg or to measure the distance from the thrombus to the deep venous junction
Overlooking an underlying malignancy in migratory thrombophlebitis
Not recognising suppurative (septic) thrombophlebitis, which needs antibiotics and possible vein excision
Providing an inadequate duration or intensity of anticoagulation for extensive or junction-related disease

CHEST guidelines on antithrombotic therapy for venous thromboembolic disease
management: Treat short-segment thrombosis remote from the deep junction with symptomatic measures such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, compression and mobilisation
Give a defined course of prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation, such as fondaparinux or low-molecular-weight heparin, for thrombosis of significant length lying away from the saphenous junctions
Use therapeutic anticoagulation as for deep vein thrombosis when thrombus lies close to or extends into the deep system
Perform whole-leg compression ultrasound to map extent, measure distance to the deep junction and exclude coexisting deep vein thrombosis
Investigate for occult malignancy or thromboangiitis obliterans in migratory or recurrent thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign), and exclude an underlying carcinoma in Mondor disease of the chest wall
Undertake a thrombophilia screen in recurrent, unprovoked or unusual-site cases
Address underlying chronic venous disease and varicosities to reduce recurrence
